summary:
The Ioway call themselves Báxoje, a name often translated as gray snow. Their language is Chiwere, part of the Siouan family. Europeans first met the Ioway at a Ho-Chunk village on Green Bay. Later the Ioway lived across what is now Iowa, from the Missouri River to the lower Des Moines River, and then in villages along the rivers of northern Missouri. Their lands once covered millions of acres, centered on the state that bears their name.

Through a long series of treaties with the United States, some of them fraudulent and all signed under pressure, the Ioway lost their homeland in Iowa and Missouri. They moved to the Great Nemaha Reservation, on what became the border of Kansas and Nebraska, and allotment later cut that land further.

Differences over farming, assimilation and allotment divided the people. Families who held to older ways moved south to Indian Territory, where an executive order set aside a reservation for them in 1883. That land, too, was allotted, and the rest was opened to settlers. Some southern families went on to join Otoe relatives near Red Rock.

Today the Ioway are two nations. The Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska bases its federal recognition on the old treaties. The Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma is headquartered near Perkins and holds an Ioway powwow each June. Both nations are buying back former reservation land with revenue from tribal enterprises.

sources.name: Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture (Oklahoma Historical Society), Iowa
Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska, Treaties

grouping_feedback: Grouping is correct. The Oklahoma Historical Society writes the self-name 'Bah-Kho-Je'. Confirm 'Báxoje' with both nations. The Otoe-Missouria (Chiwere-speaking relatives) are not in the directory. Consider a 'related peoples' link to Ho-Chunk and Otoe-Missouria once a source supports it; none of my sources named the Chiwere relatives.
notes: Only two sources, one of them tribal. I left out the first-contact year (1676), the 1839 cession date, the 1878 start of the southern move and the treaty-by-treaty dates (1815–1861 list), each on one source. Membership (496 in 2003) is outdated and left out.
